CT urography (unenhanced phase, nephrographic or venous phase and excretory phase) is the reference exam in adult gross hematuria for studying the kidneys, collecting systems and bladder. Urothelial carcinoma of the bladder appears as an exophytic mass or focal wall thickening that enhances in the venous phase and causes a filling defect when the urine is opacified.

Pitfalls: with a poorly distended bladder the wall looks thick; a clot can mimic a mass (it does not enhance and moves with patient position); the prostatic median lobe protrudes from the base in the midline; in the delayed phases layering contrast can hide lesions of the anterior wall (also look at the venous phase). Urothelial carcinoma is often multifocal: the upper urinary tract must always be checked.

CT does not stage the wall T category (Ta-T1 versus T2): the depth of invasion is defined by transurethral resection (TURBT) and by multiparametric MRI (VI-RADS). CT is used for extravesical extension (T3b-T4), lymph nodes and metastases.

In this case the mass was a high-grade urothelial carcinoma of the posterior wall, pT2a N0 M0; at cystoprostatectomy an incidental prostate adenocarcinoma (pT2a) was also found, a frequent occurrence.
